title: Sequence Builder: From Shot to Sequence

intro.heading: Build the Sequence
intro.body: Documentary form begins with a small decision: where to look, when to stay, and what must come next. Before you arrange the potter’s process, move through three scales of visual thought—shot, sequence, and scene.
intro.heroNote: One place. One contributor. One process about to begin.
intro.grammarBody: These are not merely different sizes of coverage. Each one does a different kind of documentary work. Learn to recognize the unit you are making while the camera is still rolling.

grammarUnits.definition: One continuous observation from cut to cut. A shot selects a fragment of reality and asks us to notice it: a face thinking, a foot finding the pedal, wet fingers meeting clay.
grammarUnits.potterExample: The foot presses the pedal. In one shot, cause becomes visible.
grammarUnits.question: What does this image prove?

grammarUnits.definition: Several shots joined by action, process, space, or idea. A sequence lets the viewer reconstruct how something happens—even when real time has been compressed.
grammarUnits.potterExample: Clay placed → wheel started → center opened → walls raised → bowl revealed.
grammarUnits.question: Can the viewer follow the change?

grammarUnits.definition: A scene unfolds in a particular place and present tense. It contains a dynamic: a desire, obstacle, uncertainty, encounter, or turn. A scene may hold one sequence—or several.
grammarUnits.potterExample: The potter works to hold a collapsing rim while a customer waits. Process now carries tension.
grammarUnits.question: What can change before we leave?

intro.fieldNoteHeading: The camera records shots. The filmmaker constructs meaning.
intro.fieldNoteBody: On location, do not collect images as insurance. Film the states of change: before, cause, transformation, consequence, result. Then stay awake for the human detail that turns a process into lived experience.
instructions: Arrange the images into an intelligible order.
Compare your construction with the model sequence.
Remove one shot and consider what changes.
Choose the shot you believe is indispensable.
intro.beginPrompt: Ten frames. One process. Build the visual logic.

arrange.heading: What does the viewer need to see—and when?
arrange.instruction: Drag the frames into an intelligible order, or use the move controls on each card. Build a beginning, a developing action, and a visible result.
arrange.resetMessage: The original scrambled order has been restored.

intelligible.label: Intelligible sequence
intelligible.body: Your sequence is intelligible. The action progresses clearly from setup through transformation to result. Notice how the cutaways can create rhythm and soften transitions between similar framings.

partial.label: Partly intelligible sequence
partial.body: Your sequence contains the necessary material, but part of the action is out of order. Check whether the beginning, cause, transformation, development, and result are all clearly connected.

unclear.label: Unclear sequence
unclear.body: The viewer may struggle to understand how the action develops. Begin by identifying the starting condition, what causes the wheel to move, how the clay changes, and where the process ends.

removal.heading: Test the structure
removal.instruction: Remove one shot. Then consider what becomes weaker, rougher, or less clear.
removal.selectInstruction: Select a frame, then remove it from the sequence.
removal.prompt: What changes when this shot is removed?
removal.minimumHint: Write at least 20 characters before viewing feedback.
removal.responseRequired: Write at least 20 characters about what changed.

feedback.F1: The action may still be understandable, but the viewer loses orientation. Place, contributor, and starting context are weakened.
feedback.F2: The sequence loses part of its beginning. The viewer no longer clearly sees the material before the transformation starts.
feedback.F3: Cause and effect are weakened. The viewer no longer sees what sets the wheel in motion.
feedback.F4: A major process stage is missing. The clay appears to move too quickly from setup toward transformation.
feedback.F5: A critical transformation is missing. The viewer does not clearly see how the solid clay begins to become a vessel.
feedback.F6: The sequence loses a major stage of development. The bowl appears to form without enough visual evidence of how it grew.
feedback.F7: The sequence remains intelligible, but it loses a moment of concentration and human presence. The edit may also feel more abrupt between similar action framings.
feedback.F8: The sequence loses the stage where the rough form is refined. The transition toward completion becomes less clear.
feedback.F9: The sequence remains intelligible, but the transition toward the completed bowl may feel more abrupt. The detailed craft of refining the rim is also reduced.
feedback.F10: The sequence loses its visible result. The viewer sees the process but does not clearly arrive at completion.

removal.bothCutawaysFeedback: The action can still be followed, but the sequence now feels visually abrupt. Direct cuts between similar framings create a jump-cut effect.

indispensable.heading: Name the load-bearing shot
indispensable.instruction: Select the one shot you believe the sequence would be hardest to understand without.
indispensable.minimumHint: Write at least 20 characters before viewing feedback.
indispensable.selectionRequired: Select the shot you believe is indispensable.
indispensable.responseRequired: Write at least 20 characters explaining your choice.

feedback.F1: Strong choice. This shot establishes the contributor, activity, and location before the process begins.
feedback.F2: This is a defensible choice. The shot carries an important stage of the action, and removing it would weaken the sequence’s progression.
feedback.F3: Good choice. This shot clarifies cause and effect by showing how the wheel starts moving.
feedback.F4: This is a defensible choice. The shot carries an important stage of the action, and removing it would weaken the sequence’s progression.
feedback.F5: Strong choice. This shot shows the central transformation from solid clay toward a vessel.
feedback.F6: This is a defensible choice. The shot carries an important stage of the action, and removing it would weaken the sequence’s progression.
feedback.F7: This shot is valuable, but it is more supportive than essential. It improves pacing, texture, and continuity rather than carrying the principal action.
feedback.F8: This is a defensible choice. The shot carries an important stage of the action, and removing it would weaken the sequence’s progression.
feedback.F9: This shot is valuable, but it is more supportive than essential. It improves pacing, texture, and continuity rather than carrying the principal action.
feedback.F10: Good choice. The completed bowl gives the sequence a visible result and a natural ending.

reflection.heading: Carry the sequence into your own filming
reflection.instruction: Move from this particular bowl toward a principle you can use on location.

prompts.label: What makes this a sequence rather than a collection of images?
Which shot could be removed with the least damage?
What did the cutaway shots add?
What will you pay more attention to when filming your own sequence?

summary.heading: Your sequence notes
summary.instruction: Copy or download this plain-text record for your own production notebook. Nothing is submitted to Canvas.

labels.futureAttention: What I will consider when filming

conclusion.heading: Coverage is not insurance. It is thinking in pictures.
conclusion.body: The bowl was a contained process. Documentary life will be messier: gestures overlap, access narrows, people change their minds, and the essential moment rarely announces itself. The discipline remains the same—recognize what the viewer must see, then film the relationships between those moments.

principles.title: A shot gives evidence.
principles.body: Choose a precise action, expression, object, or spatial fact. Hold long enough for its meaning to arrive.

principles.title: A sequence makes change legible.
principles.body: Film before and after, cause and effect, effort and result. Cutaways can shape rhythm, but they cannot replace missing action.

principles.title: A scene gives the change stakes.
principles.body: Look for desire, resistance, uncertainty, discovery, and consequence—the forces that make process matter to a person.

fieldNotes: Do I have the starting condition before anything changes?
Did I film the cause—not only the effect?
Can the viewer follow the transformation without explanation?
Do I have a human detail that carries attention or feeling?
Did I stay for the consequence and a visible ending?
conclusion.closingLine: A sequence answers how. A scene lets us feel why it matters.
